claim: Ultraviolet-protective compounds such as mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs) and related gadusols are produced by some bacteria, fungi, algae, and marine invertebrates.
source: Ultraviolet-protective compounds, such as mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs) and related gadusols produced by some bacteria, fungi, algae, and marine invertebrates, are critical for the survival of reef-building corals and other marine organisms exposed to high-solar irradiance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: MAAs and gadusols are critical for the survival of reef-building corals and other marine organisms exposed to high-solar irradiance.
source: Ultraviolet-protective compounds, such as mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs) and related gadusols produced by some bacteria, fungi, algae, and marine invertebrates, are critical for the survival of reef-building corals and other marine organisms exposed to high-solar irradiance.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the functional importance of these compounds.

claim: Gadusol has been found in marine fish.
source: These compounds have also been found in marine fish, where their accumulation is thought to be of dietary or symbiont origin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The accumulation of gadusol in marine fish was previously thought to be of dietary or symbiont origin.
source: These compounds have also been found in marine fish, where their accumulation is thought to be of dietary or symbiont origin.
evidence: This represents the prior understanding before the current study's findings.

claim: Fish can synthesize gadusol de novo.
source: In this study, we report the unexpected discovery that fish can synthesize gadusol de novo and that the analogous pathways are also present in amphibians, reptiles, and birds.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing gadusol production in zebrafish and expression of the pathway genes.

claim: The gadusol biosynthesis pathway is present in amphibians, reptiles, and birds.
source: In this study, we report the unexpected discovery that fish can synthesize gadusol de novo and that the analogous pathways are also present in amphibians, reptiles, and birds.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis showing EEVS and MT-Ox genes in these vertebrate classes.

claim: Engineered yeast containing fish genes can produce and secrete gadusol.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that engineered yeast containing the fish genes can produce and secrete gadusol.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with yeast expressing zebrafish EEVS and MT-Ox genes.

claim: MAAs and gadusols have been proposed to fulfill functions including sunscreen, antioxidant, stress response, intracellular nitrogen reservoir, and/or optical filter.
source: The sunscreen compounds, mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs) and related gadusols, commonly found in bacteria, fungi, algae, and marine invertebrates (Shick and Dunlap, 2002; Miyamoto et al., 2014), have been proposed to fulfill a variety of functions, such as sunscreen, antioxidant, stress response, intracellular nitrogen reservoir, and/or optical filter (Gao and Garcia-Pichel, 2011; Bok et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In cyanobacteria, MAAs are synthesized by desmethyl-4-deoxygadusol synthase (DDGS), a dehydroquinate synthase (DHQS) homolog.
source: Although their formation had long been proposed to originate from the shikimate pathway, more recent bioinformatic and biochemical studies revealed that in cyanobacteria, MAAs are synthesized by desmethyl-4-deoxygadusol synthase (DDGS), a dehydroquinate synthase (DHQS) homolog (Wu et al., 2007; Balskus and Walsh, 2010; Singh et al., 2010; Asamizu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: Inactivation of the DDGS gene in Anabaena variabilis ATCC 29413 did not abolish the production of MAAs.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of the DDGS gene in Anabaena variabilis ATCC 29413 did not abolish the production of MAAs, suggesting that additional pathways exist for the biosynthesis of MAAs (Spence et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: DDGS converts sedoheptulose 7-phosphate (SH7P) to desmethyl-4-deoxygadusol via a unique sequence of dephosphorylation, aldol condensation, enolization, dehydration, reduction, and tautomerization reactions.
source: DDGS converts sedoheptulose 7-phosphate (SH7P) to desmethyl-4-deoxygadusol via a unique sequence of dephosphorylation, aldol condensation, enolization, dehydration, reduction, and tautomerization reactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Balskus and Walsh, 2010; Asamizu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Desmethyl-4-deoxygadusol is subsequently converted by a methyltransferase to 4-deoxygadusol, the building block of MAAs.
source: The product is subsequently converted by a methyltransferase to 4-deoxygadusol, the building block of MAAs.
evidence: This is stated as part of the known MAA biosynthesis pathway.

claim: 4-Deoxygadusol has been proposed to be the precursor of gadusol.
source: 4-Deoxygadusol has also been proposed to be the precursor of gadusol (Starcevic et al., 2010; Rosic and Dove, 2011), a related compound initially isolated from cod roe (Gadus morhua L.) (Plack et al., 1981), but also found in roes of other marine fish (Plack et al., 1981; Arbeloa et al., 2010), sea urchin eggs (Chioccara et al., 1986), cysts and nauplii of brine shrimp (Grant et al., 1985), mantis shrimp crystalline cones (Bok et al., 2014), and sponges (Bandaranayake et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gadusol was initially isolated from cod roe (Gadus morhua L.).
source: 4-Deoxygadusol has also been proposed to be the precursor of gadusol (Starcevic et al., 2010; Rosic and Dove, 2011), a related compound initially isolated from cod roe (Gadus morhua L.) (Plack et al., 1981), but also found in roes of other marine fish (Plack et al., 1981; Arbeloa et al., 2010), sea urchin eggs (Chioccara et al., 1986), cysts and nauplii of brine shrimp (Grant et al., 1985), mantis shrimp crystalline cones (Bok et al., 2014), and sponges (Bandaranayake et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original isolation study.

claim: Gadusol has been found in roes of marine fish, sea urchin eggs, cysts and nauplii of brine shrimp, mantis shrimp crystalline cones, and sponges.
source: 4-Deoxygadusol has also been proposed to be the precursor of gadusol (Starcevic et al., 2010; Rosic and Dove, 2011), a related compound initially isolated from cod roe (Gadus morhua L.) (Plack et al., 1981), but also found in roes of other marine fish (Plack et al., 1981; Arbeloa et al., 2010), sea urchin eggs (Chioccara et al., 1986), cysts and nauplii of brine shrimp (Grant et al., 1985), mantis shrimp crystalline cones (Bok et al., 2014), and sponges (Bandaranayake et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting gadusol in various organisms.

claim: Genes responsible for the production of 4-deoxygadusol and MAAs are commonly found in bacteria, algae, and other marine microorganisms.
source: As genes responsible for the production of 4-deoxygadusol and MAAs are commonly found in bacteria (e.g., cyanobacteria), algae, and other marine microorganisms (Shick and Dunlap, 2002; Miyamoto et al., 2014), the accumulation of these compounds in marine animals has been proposed to be of dietary or symbiont origin (Arbeloa et al., 2010; Gao and Garcia-Pichel, 2011; Loew, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A gene cluster encoding a four-step DDGS-based pathway for converting SH7P to MAAs was discovered in the genomes of coral (Acropora digitifera) and sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis).
source: On the other hand, a gene cluster like that in cyanobacteria apparently encoding a four-step DDGS-based pathway for converting SH7P to MAAs was discovered in the genomes of a coral (Acropora digitifera) and sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis), suggesting that these invertebrates can produce MAAs autonomously (Rosic and Dove, 2011; Shinzato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: Coral (Acropora digitifera) and sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis) can produce MAAs autonomously.
source: On the other hand, a gene cluster like that in cyanobacteria apparently encoding a four-step DDGS-based pathway for converting SH7P to MAAs was discovered in the genomes of a coral (Acropora digitifera) and sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis), suggesting that these invertebrates can produce MAAs autonomously (Rosic and Dove, 2011; Shinzato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of the biosynthetic gene cluster in their genomes.

claim: DDGS is a member of the sugar phosphate cyclase (SPC) superfamily.
source: DDGS is a member of the sugar phosphate cyclase (SPC) superfamily (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The SPC superfamily includes DHQS, EEVS, EVS, aminoDHQS, and DOIS.
source: In addition to DHQS, this superfamily includes four enzymes known for their roles in the biosynthesis of natural products with therapeutic application: 2-epi-5-epi-valiolone synthase (EEVS), 2-epi-valiolone synthase, aminoDHQS, and 2-deoxy-scyllo-inosose synthase (DOIS) (Wu et al., 2007; Mahmud, 2009; Asamizu et al., 2012; Kang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EEVS catalyzes the entry step to the biosynthesis of pseudosugar-containing natural products such as acarbose and validamycin A.
source: EEVS catalyzes the entry step to the biosynthesis of pseudosugar-containing natural products, such as the antidiabetic drug acarbose and the crop protectant validamycin A, and has so far only been identified and characterized in bacteria (Mahmud, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Prior to this study, EEVS had only been identified and characterized in bacteria.
source: EEVS catalyzes the entry step to the biosynthesis of pseudosugar-containing natural products, such as the antidiabetic drug acarbose and the crop protectant validamycin A, and has so far only been identified and characterized in bacteria (Mahmud, 2009).
evidence: This represents the state of knowledge before the current study.

claim: Genes encoding EEVS-like proteins (annotated as 'PREDICTED: pentafunctional AROM polypeptide-like') were found in the genomes of fish, amphibians, reptiles, and birds.
source: Recently, we surprisingly also found genes that encode EEVS-like proteins (annotated as 'PREDICTED: pentafunctional AROM polypeptide-like') in the genomes of fish, amphibians, reptiles, and birds (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis and shown in figures and tables.

claim: The EEVS-like gene is located in a cluster with the MT-Ox gene and flanked by transcription factor genes encoding FRMD4B, MitF, MDFIC, and FoxP1.
source: This gene is located in a cluster with another functionally unknown gene (labeled as MT-Ox hereafter) and flanked by a suite of transcription factor genes encoding FRMD4B, MitF, MDFIC, and FoxP1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B depicting the genetic organization.

claim: FRMD4B, MitF, MDFIC, and FoxP1 transcription factors regulate the expression of genes with essential roles in cell differentiation, proliferation, and survival.
source: These transcription factors have been known to regulate the expression of genes with essential roles in cell differentiation, proliferation, and survival (Levy et al., 2006; Rice et al., 2012; Garner et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The zebrafish protein encoded by LOC100003999 is an EEVS that converts SH7P to EEV.
source: Incubation of the recombinant protein with SH7P gave a product, which was confirmed by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) and GC-MS to be EEV (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplements 3, 4), identifying the protein as an EEVS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data including TLC and GC-MS analysis.

claim: All animal EEVS-like proteins are highly similar (60–72% identity) and match the sequence of bacterial ValA at all 14 fingerprint sites.
source: Further supporting the assignment of the LOC100003999-encoded protein as an EEVS, sequence comparisons show that all animal EEVS-like proteins are highly similar (60–72% identity) and also match the sequence of ValA at all 14 fingerprint sites (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 5, 6).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in figures.

claim: The zebrafish MT-Ox protein (zgc:113054) is predicted to contain two domains: an N-terminal SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain and a C-terminal NAD+-dependent oxidoreductase domain.
source: The second gene, MT-Ox (zgc:113054), is predicted to encode a protein that contains two domains: the N-terminal domain is similar to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)–dependent methyltransferases, and the C-terminal domain is similar to NAD+-dependent oxidoreductases.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction of protein domains.

claim: Transcription of the zebrafish MT-Ox gene (zgc:113054) in larvae is upregulated by light.
source: Although its function in zebrafish is unknown, the transcription of this gene in larvae is upregulated by light, leading to a prediction of its involvement in circadian clock regulation (Weger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Recombinant MT-Ox protein converts EEV to gadusol in the presence of SAM and NAD+.
source: To test this hypothesis, recombinant MT-Ox protein encoded by zgc:113054 was incubated with EEV in the presence of SAM and NAD+. Following incubation, a product with λmax of 294 nm (pH 7) and 270 (pH 2.5) was detected (Figure 2A–B). Further analysis of the product by (−)-ESI-MS (m/z 203 [M-H]−) and 1H NMR confirmed its identity as gadusol (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data including UV spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, and NMR.

claim: The conversion of EEV to gadusol by MT-Ox takes place via oxidation of the C-2 or C-3 OH, followed by enolization and methylation of the resulting C-2 OH.
source: We postulate that the conversion of EEV to gadusol by MT-Ox takes place via oxidation of the C-2 or C-3 OH, followed by enolization and methylation of the resulting C-2 OH (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the substrate and product structures.

claim: The pathway to gadusol in vertebrates is distinct from the pathway used in the biosynthesis of MAAs.
source: This new pathway to the UV-absorbing vinylogous acid functional group shared by gadusol and 4-deoxygadusol is distinct from that used in the biosynthesis of the MAAs (Balskus and Walsh, 2010; Spence et al., 2012), and the existence of multiple pathways for generating this scaffold is intriguing and may indicate that this is a privileged chemical scaffold in living organisms.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the enzymatic mechanisms and supported by citations.

claim: Both the LOC100003999 and zgc:113054 genes are expressed during zebrafish embryonic development.
source: In zebrafish, both of the LOC100003999 and zgc:113054 genes are expressed during embryonic development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Expression of LOC100003999 and zgc:113054 genes in zebrafish embryos is maximal at 72 hours post-fertilization (hpf).
source: qRT-PCR analysis of mRNA isolated from zebrafish embryos at 12, 24, 48, 72, 96, and 120 hpf showed maximal expression at 72 hpf (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Gadusol was detected in zebrafish embryo extracts collected at 72 hpf.
source: To demonstrate de novo synthesis of gadusol in zebrafish, the embryos were collected at 72 hpf, lyophilized and extracted with methanol, and the extract was analyzed by HPLC and ESI-MS (Figure 2G). Our finding of gadusol in the extract unambiguously confirms the ability of zebrafish to synthesize gadusol and amends the current perception that gadusol found in fish and other vertebrates is necessarily of dietary or symbiont origin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HPLC and ESI-MS analysis of zebrafish embryo extracts.

claim: Zebrafish can synthesize gadusol de novo.
source: Our finding of gadusol in the extract unambiguously confirms the ability of zebrafish to synthesize gadusol and amends the current perception that gadusol found in fish and other vertebrates is necessarily of dietary or symbiont origin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by detection of gadusol in zebrafish embryo extracts.

claim: There is no evidence that fish have the biosynthetic enzymes for MAAs.
source: However, as MAAs are synthesized via a different pathway and there is no evidence that fish have those biosynthetic enzymes, the accumulation of MAAs in fish would still appear to be of dietary origin (Mason et al., 1998; Zamzow, 2004).
evidence: This is based on the absence of MAA biosynthetic genes in fish genomes and supported by citations.

claim: The accumulation of MAAs in fish is of dietary origin.
source: However, as MAAs are synthesized via a different pathway and there is no evidence that fish have those biosynthetic enzymes, the accumulation of MAAs in fish would still appear to be of dietary origin (Mason et al., 1998; Zamzow, 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of MAA biosynthetic genes in fish and supported by citations.

claim: Engineered yeast with deleted TAL1 gene and expressing zebrafish LOC100003999 and zgc:113054 genes can produce and secrete gadusol.
source: To show that the recombinant LOC100003999 and zgc:113054 genes are sufficient for encoding gadusol synthesis, they were cloned into a yeast expression vector and transferred into a Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain, in which the transaldolase gene TAL1 had been deleted. Yeast possesses a robust pentose–phosphate pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and by removing the transaldolase enzyme, which normally metabolizes SH7P, and adding EEVS and MT-Ox, we expected to facilitate an effective shunt pathway from SH7P to gadusol. Analysis of the culture broth by HPLC, ESI-MS, and UV spectrophotometry revealed the presence of gadusol (Figure 2H) and its accumulation to ∼20 mg/l after 5 days (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing gadusol production in engineered yeast.

claim: Gadusol accumulates to approximately 20 mg/l in engineered yeast cultures after 5 days.
source: Analysis of the culture broth by HPLC, ESI-MS, and UV spectrophotometry revealed the presence of gadusol (Figure 2H) and its accumulation to ∼20 mg/l after 5 days (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Gadusol-containing supernatant suppresses the UVB-sensitivity of a yeast rad1∆ mutant.
source: To test the UV-protective activity of gadusol, a yeast rad1∆ mutant, which is sensitive to UVB, was suspended at approximately 107 cells/mL in the concentrated supernatant from the gadusol-producing yeast strain or from an otherwise isogenic control strain that did not produce gadusol. The gadusol-containing supernatant suppressed the UVB-sensitivity of the rad1∆ mutant (Figure 2I), confirming the UVB-protective activity of gadusol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing increased survival of rad1∆ mutant yeast exposed to UVB in the presence of gadusol.

claim: Gadusol has UVB-protective activity.
source: The gadusol-containing supernatant suppressed the UVB-sensitivity of the rad1∆ mutant (Figure 2I), confirming the UVB-protective activity of gadusol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing protection against UVB damage.

claim: Gadusol increases the UVB tolerance of wild-type (RAD1) yeast strain.
source: Analogous experiments with a wild-type strain (RAD1) at higher doses of UVB showed comparable results (Figure 2J), consistent with UVB protective activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The vertebrate EEVS and MT-Ox genes were most plausibly acquired via horizontal gene transfer.
source: As noted above, the SPCs EEVS, EVS, DDGS, aminoDHQS, and DOIS are all related to DHQS and are widespread in bacteria and fungi, but other than this report, are not known to exist in vertebrates or prevertebrates. We suggest that the vertebrate EEVS and MT-Ox genes were most plausibly acquired via horizontal gene transfer.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of these genes and the absence in prevertebrates.

claim: Aureococcus anophagefferens and Coccomyxa subellipsoidea are the only non-vertebrate organisms in current databases that harbor a similar bifunctional MT-Ox gene adjacent to a predicted EEVS gene.
source: Interestingly, searches identify the stramenopile Aureococcus anophagefferens and the microalgae Coccomyxa subellipsoidea, as the only non-vertebrate organisms in current databases that harbor a similar bifunctional MT-Ox gene, and both organisms have a predicted EEVS gene adjacent to that of MT-Ox.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic searches of genomic databases.

claim: Algae are known to be active horizontal gene transfer agents.
source: As algae are known to be active horizontal gene transfer agents (Ni et al., 2012), algae such as these become a plausible place both for the development of this alternate pathway for gadusol production and as a source of the genes found in vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Aureococcus anophagefferens EEVS protein is substantially more similar to vertebrate EEVSs than to bacterial EEVSs.
source: Further supporting such a relationship, the A. anophagefferens EEVS protein is substantially more similar to the vertebrate EEVSs than it is to bacterial EEVSs (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, denoted by the blue star).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic trees in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tunicates and lancelets lack the EEVS and MT-Ox genes.
source: Further bioinformatics studies also showed that the tunicates and lancelets lack the EEVS and MT-Ox genes, suggesting that the gene transfer occurred sometime during the evolution of primitive chordates to bony fishes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: The horizontal gene transfer of EEVS and MT-Ox occurred sometime during the evolution of primitive chordates to bony fishes.
source: Further bioinformatics studies also showed that the tunicates and lancelets lack the EEVS and MT-Ox genes, suggesting that the gene transfer occurred sometime during the evolution of primitive chordates to bony fishes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of the genes.

claim: The EEVS and MT-Ox genes are retained in modern ray-finned fish (with the exception of puffer fish), amphibians, reptiles, and birds.
source: While the EEVS and MT-Ox genes are retained in modern ray-finned fish (with the exception of puffer fish), as well as in amphibians, reptiles, and birds, they were lost in mammals, including the egg-laying mammal platypus, indicating the lack of a direct link between gadusol and the mode of reproduction.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Puffer fish lack the EEVS and MT-Ox genes.
source: While the EEVS and MT-Ox genes are retained in modern ray-finned fish (with the exception of puffer fish), as well as in amphibians, reptiles, and birds, they were lost in mammals, including the egg-laying mammal platypus, indicating the lack of a direct link between gadusol and the mode of reproduction.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The EEVS and MT-Ox genes were lost in mammals, including the egg-laying mammal platypus.
source: While the EEVS and MT-Ox genes are retained in modern ray-finned fish (with the exception of puffer fish), as well as in amphibians, reptiles, and birds, they were lost in mammals, including the egg-laying mammal platypus, indicating the lack of a direct link between gadusol and the mode of reproduction.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: There is no direct link between gadusol biosynthesis capability and the mode of reproduction.
source: While the EEVS and MT-Ox genes are retained in modern ray-finned fish (with the exception of puffer fish), as well as in amphibians, reptiles, and birds, they were lost in mammals, including the egg-laying mammal platypus, indicating the lack of a direct link between gadusol and the mode of reproduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that the egg-laying platypus lacks the genes while egg-laying birds and reptiles retain them.

claim: The West African coelacanth genome appears to lack the EEVS and MT-Ox genes.
source: The West African coelacanth genome (Amemiya et al., 2013) also appears to lack the EEVS and MT-Ox genes (Figure 3, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the coelacanth genome.

claim: The West African coelacanth is a rare ovoviviparous fish that lives in caves 100–500 meters deep and feeds at night.
source: This rare ovoviviparous fish lives in caves 100–500 meters deep and feeds at night, and its lack of gadusol production ability may be directly related to its limited exposure to UV light and/or oxidative stress.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the coelacanth's ecology.

claim: The coelacanth's lack of gadusol production ability may be directly related to its limited exposure to UV light and/or oxidative stress.
source: This rare ovoviviparous fish lives in caves 100–500 meters deep and feeds at night, and its lack of gadusol production ability may be directly related to its limited exposure to UV light and/or oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the coelacanth's ecology and lack of EEVS/MT-Ox genes.

claim: Gadusol is present in fish eggs where it can serve to protect the roe from UV damage.
source: Other than the well-documented presence of gadusol in fish eggs, where it can serve to protect the roe from UV damage (Arbeloa et al., 2010; Colleter et al., 2014), nothing is known of its role(s) in fish, reptiles, amphibians, and birds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nothing is known of gadusol's role(s) in fish, reptiles, amphibians, and birds beyond its presence in fish eggs.
source: Other than the well-documented presence of gadusol in fish eggs, where it can serve to protect the roe from UV damage (Arbeloa et al., 2010; Colleter et al., 2014), nothing is known of its role(s) in fish, reptiles, amphibians, and birds.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The zebrafish EEVS-like protein (LOC100003999) was expressed as a recombinant protein in E. coli.
source: To investigate the function of the vertebrate EEVS-like genes, the protein encoded by the zebrafish EEVS-like gene (LOC100003999) was expressed in Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is described in the methods and results sections.

claim: The crystal structure of bacterial EEVS ValA (PDB entry 4P53) allowed identification of a fingerprint set of 14 active-site residues that differentiate various SH7P cyclases.
source: The best-characterized bacterial EEVS is ValA from the validamycin pathway in Streptomyces hygroscopicus subsp. jinggangensis 5008 (Bai et al., 2006), and the crystal structure of ValA (Protein Data Bank [PDB] entry 4P53) (Kean et al., 2014), allowed identification of a fingerprint set of 14 active-site residues with characteristic variations that could differentiate the various SH7P cyclases.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of ValA and supported by citations.

claim: Yeast possesses a robust pentose-phosphate pathway.
source: Yeast possesses a robust pentose–phosphate pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and by removing the transaldolase enzyme, which normally metabolizes SH7P, and adding EEVS and MT-Ox, we expected to facilitate an effective shunt pathway from SH7P to gadusol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast metabolism and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Transaldolase enzyme normally metabolizes SH7P in yeast.
source: Yeast possesses a robust pentose–phosphate pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and by removing the transaldolase enzyme, which normally metabolizes SH7P, and adding EEVS and MT-Ox, we expected to facilitate an effective shunt pathway from SH7P to gadusol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pentose phosphate pathway.

claim: Removing transaldolase and adding EEVS and MT-Ox facilitates an effective shunt pathway from SH7P to gadusol in yeast.
source: Yeast possesses a robust pentose–phosphate pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and by removing the transaldolase enzyme, which normally metabolizes SH7P, and adding EEVS and MT-Ox, we expected to facilitate an effective shunt pathway from SH7P to gadusol.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested and confirmed by the experimental results showing gadusol production.

claim: Gadusol has a λmax of 294 nm at pH 7 and 270 nm at pH 2.5.
source: Following incubation, a product with λmax of 294 nm (pH 7) and 270 (pH 2.5) was detected (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is measured experimentally by UV spectroscopy.

claim: The enzymatic product of MT-Ox acting on EEV has a molecular ion at m/z 203 [M-H]− by ESI-MS.
source: Further analysis of the product by (−)-ESI-MS (m/z 203 [M-H]−) and 1H NMR confirmed its identity as gadusol (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This is measured experimentally by mass spectrometry.

claim: The existence of multiple pathways for generating the UV-absorbing vinylogous acid functional group may indicate that this is a privileged chemical scaffold in living organisms.
source: This new pathway to the UV-absorbing vinylogous acid functional group shared by gadusol and 4-deoxygadusol is distinct from that used in the biosynthesis of the MAAs (Balskus and Walsh, 2010; Spence et al., 2012), and the existence of multiple pathways for generating this scaffold is intriguing and may indicate that this is a privileged chemical scaffold in living organisms.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding of multiple biosynthetic pathways.

claim: The discovery of the gadusol pathway in vertebrates provides a platform for understanding its role in these animals.
source: The discovery of the gadusol pathway in vertebrates provides a platform for understanding its role in these animals, and the possibility of engineering yeast to efficiently produce a natural sunscreen and antioxidant presents an avenue for its large-scale production for possible use in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Engineering yeast to produce gadusol presents an avenue for large-scale production for possible use in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.
source: The discovery of the gadusol pathway in vertebrates provides a platform for understanding its role in these animals, and the possibility of engineering yeast to efficiently produce a natural sunscreen and antioxidant presents an avenue for its large-scale production for possible use in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications based on the demonstration of gadusol production in engineered yeast.

claim: Gadusol has antioxidant properties.
source: The results not only demonstrate the ability of the engineered yeast to produce and secrete gadusol but also present a new avenue for large-scale production of the compound for possible commercial uses, for example, sunscreen and/or antioxidant (Plack et al., 1981; Schmid et al., 2006; Cardozo et al., 2007; Arbeloa et al., 2010).

claim: Gadusol has sunscreen properties.
